subject: SLO hypothesis check-in — windowing, streaming, and perf trade-offs
messages:
From: Ava Chen <ava@redwoodinference.com>
To: Helen Park <helen@brightline.ai>, Markus Ekstrom <markus@brightline.ai>
Cc: Priyom Das <priyom_das@redwoodinference.com>, Marissa Cole <marissa_cole@redwoodinference.com>
Date: Fri, 02 Apr 2027 15:12:00 -0700
Subject: SLO hypothesis check-in — windowing, streaming, and perf trade-offs

Hi Helen / Markus,

Thanks again for taking time today — good discussion. Short recap and concrete asks so we can validate hypotheses before the next technical deep dive with infra: 

1) Target SLOs you mentioned: 95th percentile latency at <= 180ms for short inference (<=1k tokens output) and 95th <= 400ms for heavy responses (combined input+output up to ~12k tokens). Please confirm if those buckets are accurate.

2) Expected QPS / concurrency: you said typical steady-state is ~40 qps with spikes to 120 qps, and a max concurrent sessions target of ~10. Are those burst windows <5 minutes? That matters for autoscaling.

3) Streaming: you want token-by-token output for chat playback with <50ms inter-token arrival. In our experience that tight inter-token SLO is sensitive to (a) sequence length (larger context causes slower decode per token), (b) KV cache warmups on de-duped requests, and (c) network chunking. Are there UX constraints for initial token latency vs sustained inter-token latency?

4) Context windows: you listed a working set of 8–12k input tokens (docs + user history) and 1–2k output tokens. We flagged two operational knock-ons: increased P95 from longer cross-attention steps, and higher memory footprint impacting colocated batching. Would you be open to a graceful degrade path (pin shorter context for low-latency routes + background longer-context rerank)?

Next steps I propose:
- You confirm the three numbers above (SLO buckets, QPS burst profile, streaming inter-token tolerance)
- We run a short worksheet (attached) to map their sample prompts -> expected token counts and classify into latency buckets
- Technical deep dive (30–45m) next week with our infra/serving lead (Priyom) to sketch autoscale and fallback policies

I've attached a concise SLO worksheet and our call recording for reference. If you can drop the sample payload sizes (typical user prompt + doc sizes) into the sheet, Priyom and I can produce a quick set of recommended configs (batch sizes, quantization/throughput trade-offs, and streaming chunking) by EOD Friday.

Thanks —
Ava Chen
Principal Solutions Engineer, Redwood Inference
ava@redwoodinference.com | +1 (415) 555-0123

Subject: Re: SLO hypothesis check-in — windowing, streaming, and perf trade-offs

Ava — thanks for the summary and for capturing the asks. Quick clarifications inline:

1) SLO buckets: yes, the 180ms / 400ms P95 are correct as customer-facing targets. Internally we can tolerate higher P99 for complex sessions but we want the P95 to be tight.

2) QPS: steady-state is 35–45 qps. Bursts to ~120 are for marketing-driven spikes and last ~3–8 minutes historically. Concurrency cap of ~10 is right for active “session” objects.

3) Streaming: our main UX requirement is perceived responsiveness — first token under ~250ms is acceptable if per-token streaming thereafter is smooth (~40–60ms). So we can trade a slightly higher first-byte for better inter-token rhythm.

4) Context windows: typical doc ingestion per session is 6–10k tokens; some enterprise customers push to 16k for legal threads but those are <5% of sessions. We are open to a degrade pattern that keeps interactive chat sub-1k context fast and pushes long-context operations into a queued path with progress/event streaming.

I'll populate the worksheet with a few real payloads by EOD. Also looping our infra PM Markus to coordinate the deep technical call.

—Helen
Helen Park
Head of Product, Brightline AI
helen@brightline.ai

Subject: Re: SLO hypothesis check-in — windowing, streaming, and perf trade-offs

Hi all — quickly jumping in with the infra angle and a first-pass of trade-offs based on Helen's clarifications: 

- First-token vs inter-token: given their tolerance, we can prioritize steady streaming once the decoder loop is warmed. Practically that means we may accept ~200–300ms initial latency for sessions with large attention windows to guarantee ~40–60ms inter-token when using continuous decoding on GPU.

- Batching & concurrency: for their 40 qps steady-state with 120 qps spikes, we recommend a mixed-policy: a latency-first lane (pin requests to small-batch, low-latency workers) and a throughput lane (larger-batch, quantized models) for non-urgent long-context jobs. Autoscale: keep a warm pool sized for 1.5x steady qps and allow fast burst capacity via preemptible instances. This keeps cold-start impact on P95 bounded.

- Context window handling: for sessions with <= 10k combined tokens, a single high-precision variant on A100/RTX8000-class nodes should hit the P95 targets in our microbenchmarks. For the 12–16k tail we propose: (a) prefix-KV caching for repeated doc references, (b) segmented pass where we compress older history (vector summaries) before attention, or (c) soft-fallback to a background rerank flow. We'll sketch CPU/RAM sizing for each approach in the deep dive.

Action items from infra:
1) Priyom to run two short microbenchmarks (1k output / 2k output) against a representative 10k-context synthetic workload by Wednesday and post results to the Drive link.
2) Ava/Marissa to collect 5 sample session payloads from Brightline and drop into the worksheet by EOD Tuesday.
3) Schedule technical deep dive (45m) — suggested slots Wed/Thu next week.

I'll attach a quick microbenchmark plan to the Drive folder.

—Priyom

Quick note for the call: please be prepared to show one example long-context session so we can walk through fallback UX expectations (what gets truncated, what gets backgrounded, and the user-visible retry behavior).

Talk soon —
Ava
